chapters.n: This book is a revelation from Jesus Christ, given by the Father and delivered through an angel to John. “Revelation” translates the Greek apokalypsis—an unveiling of hidden things.

f.g: Greek apokalypsis — uncovering, unveiling.
Traditionally the Apostle John.

chapters.n: John faithfully recorded God’s word, Christ’s testimony, and everything he saw in vision.

f.g: Testified, bore witness.

chapters.n: The first of seven “blessed” sayings in Revelation: those who read this prophecy aloud, those who hear it, and those who live by it will be blessed.

f.g: In early churches one person read scripture aloud to the congregation.

chapters.n: John greets seven real congregations in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey). The blessing comes from the eternal God and from the “seven Spirits” before His throne—seven being a number of completeness.

f.w: seven churches which are in Asia
f.g: Seven cities in the Roman province of Asia, not the continent.

f.w: which is, and which was, and which is to come

chapters.n: Grace also comes from Jesus Christ: the faithful witness, the first to rise from the dead, and ruler of earth’s kings. John praises Him who loves us and washed away our sins with His own blood.

f.w: washed us from our sins in his own blood

chapters.n: Christ has made His followers kings and priests to serve God. Latter-day Saints associate this with temple blessings and exaltation.
Christ will come again in the clouds, and everyone will see Him—even those who pierced Him. All earth’s peoples will mourn.
The Lord declares that He is Alpha and Omega—the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet. He is the beginning and the end, the Almighty.
John describes himself as a fellow believer sharing their suffering. He had been banished to Patmos, a small rocky island in the Aegean Sea, because of his testimony.

f.g: A small island off the coast of modern Turkey, used by Rome for exile.

chapters.n: On the Lord’s day—Sunday, the day of Christ’s Resurrection—John was caught up in the Spirit and heard a voice behind him loud as a trumpet.
The voice told John to write what he saw and send it to seven named churches. The cities lie roughly in a circle, in the order a messenger would travel.

f.g: A scroll.
The last stop on the circuit, near Colossae.

chapters.n: Turning toward the voice, John saw seven golden lampstands.

f.g: Lampstands holding oil lamps, not candles.

chapters.n: Among the lampstands stood one like the Son of Man—Jesus—in a long robe with a golden sash across His chest, like a priest or king.

f.g: Chest, breast.
Belt or sash.

chapters.n: His hair was white as wool and snow, and His eyes blazed like fire. These images show purity, eternal wisdom, and the power to see through everything.
His feet glowed like polished bronze in a furnace, and His voice sounded like a roaring waterfall. Joseph Smith described the resurrected Lord in the Kirtland Temple in similar terms.

f.g: Burnished bronze.

chapters.n: He held seven stars in His right hand, a sharp two-edged sword came from His mouth, and His face shone like the noonday sun.

f.g: His word, which judges and cuts to the heart.

chapters.n: John collapsed like a dead man. Jesus touched him and said, “Don’t be afraid. I am the first and the last.”

f.w: fell at his feet as dead

chapters.n: Jesus declares that He died and now lives forever, holding the keys of death and hell. Because of Him, death and the spirit prison will not have the last word.

f.w: keys of hell and of death
f.g: hell = Greek hadēs, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: Christ tells John to write what he has seen, what currently is, and what will happen later.
Jesus explains the symbols: the seven stars are the “angels” or messengers of the churches—likely their leaders—and the lampstands are the churches themselves, which are to give light.

f.g: Greek angelos — messenger; probably the presiding officers of each congregation.

chapters.n: Christ dictates a letter to the church at Ephesus, a large port city and home of the famous temple of Artemis. He presents Himself as the one who holds the leaders and walks among the churches.

f.g: He is present with and watches over His churches.

chapters.n: Christ praises their hard work, endurance, and refusal to tolerate evil. They tested people who falsely claimed to be apostles and exposed them.

f.w: say they are apostles, and are not

chapters.n: They have endured hardships for Christ’s name and have not grown weary.

f.g: Grown weary, given up.

chapters.n: But Christ has a concern: they have abandoned the love they had at first. Correct doctrine without love is not enough.
Remember how far you have fallen, repent, and do what you did at first. Otherwise Christ will remove their lampstand—they would cease to be His church.

f.g: Their standing as a light-bearing church would be taken away.

chapters.n: Still, they rightly hate the practices of the Nicolaitans, which Christ hates too. The Nicolaitans were apparently a group that compromised with idolatry and immorality.

f.g: A sect whose exact teachings are uncertain; linked with the ‘doctrine of Balaam’ in verses 14-15.

chapters.n: Each letter ends with a call to listen and a promise. Whoever overcomes will eat from the tree of life in God’s paradise—access lost in Eden restored.
To Smyrna (modern İzmir), Christ speaks as the One who died and came back to life—fitting for a church facing death.

f.g: A wealthy port city known for loyalty to Rome and emperor worship.

chapters.n: Christ knows their suffering and poverty, but says they are truly rich. Some local opponents claim God’s covenant but act as Satan’s assembly by slandering believers.

f.g: A sharp label for local opponents who persecuted the believers.

chapters.n: Don’t fear coming suffering. Some will be imprisoned for a short, limited time—“ten days.” Be faithful even to death, and Christ will give you the crown of life.

f.g: Probably a brief, limited period.

chapters.n: Those who overcome will not be harmed by the second death—final spiritual separation from God.
To Pergamos, Christ speaks as the One with the sharp two-edged sword. Pergamos was a seat of Roman government, which held the ‘right of the sword’—but Christ’s sword is greater.

f.g: Pergamum, a provincial center of Roman power and emperor worship.

chapters.n: They live where “Satan’s seat” is—perhaps the great altar of Zeus or the emperor-worship temple. Yet they stayed loyal even when Antipas was martyred there.

f.g: A faithful martyr otherwise unknown.
Greek martys — witness.

chapters.n: But some follow the “doctrine of Balaam,” who advised King Balak to lure Israel into idolatry and immorality. Similar compromises were creeping in.

f.g: Balak, king of Moab.

chapters.n: Some also hold to the Nicolaitans’ teaching, which Christ hates.
Repent, or Christ will come and fight such teachers with the sword of His word.
Overcomers will receive hidden manna—heavenly food—and a white stone with a new name only the receiver knows. Latter-day Saints connect the white stone to a Urim and Thummim given to celestial heirs.
To Thyatira, a trade city famous for guilds, Christ speaks as the Son of God with eyes of fire and feet of bronze.

f.g: A city of trade guilds; Lydia the seller of purple came from here.

chapters.n: Christ commends their love, service, faith, and endurance—and notes they are doing even more now than at first.

f.w: the last to be more than the first
f.g: Their recent works exceed their earlier ones.

chapters.n: But they tolerate a woman, nicknamed “Jezebel” after Ahab’s idolatrous queen, who claims to be a prophetess and leads people into immorality and idol feasts.
Christ gave her time to repent, but she refused.
Her bed of sin will become a bed of suffering, and her followers will face great distress unless they repent.

f.g: A bed of sickness or affliction.

chapters.n: Her spiritual children will die, and all the churches will know Christ searches minds and hearts and repays each by their works.

f.g: Kidneys—seat of deepest feelings and thoughts.

chapters.n: To the faithful in Thyatira who rejected this teaching and the so-called “deep secrets of Satan,” Christ adds no further burden.

f.g: Perhaps the false teachers boasted of ‘deep’ knowledge.

chapters.n: Just hold on to what you have until He comes.
Whoever overcomes and keeps Christ’s works to the end will share His authority over the nations.
He will rule with an iron scepter, shattering resistance like pottery, just as Christ received from His Father. The JST renders this as ruling with the word of God.
Christ will also give him the morning star—Christ Himself.
Listen to what the Spirit is saying to the churches—these messages apply to us too.
To Sardis, a once-proud city with a fading reputation, Christ says: you have a name for being alive, but you are dead. Reputation is not the same as spiritual life.

f.g: Former capital of Lydia, famous for wealth but past its glory.

chapters.n: Wake up and strengthen what little is left before it dies; your works aren’t complete in God’s sight.

f.g: Sardis was twice captured because its guards failed to watch.

chapters.n: Remember what you received, keep it, and repent. If you don’t wake up, Christ will come unexpectedly, like a thief.
A few in Sardis have kept their clothes clean, and they will walk with Christ in white because they are worthy.
Overcomers will be dressed in white. Christ will never erase their names from the book of life, and He will acknowledge them before His Father and angels.
Listen to what the Spirit says to the churches.
To Philadelphia, Christ is the Holy and True One who holds the key of David—authority to open and shut that no one can override.

f.g: Name means ‘brotherly love’; a small city often shaken by earthquakes.

chapters.n: Christ has placed an open door before them that no one can shut. Though they have little strength, they kept His word and didn’t deny Him.
Their persecutors will one day bow before them and recognize that Christ loves them.
Because they patiently kept His word, Christ will protect them in the time of testing coming on the whole world.

f.g: A time of trial or testing.

chapters.n: Christ is coming soon. Hold on to what you have so no one can take your crown.

Overcomers will become pillars in God’s temple, never to leave. Christ will write on them God’s name, the name of the New Jerusalem, and His own new name. In earthquake-prone Philadelphia, a stable pillar was a powerful image.
Listen to what the Spirit says to the churches.
To Laodicea, Christ speaks as the Amen—the One whose word is sure—the faithful witness, and the source of God’s creation.

f.w: beginning of the creation of God
f.g: The origin or ruler of creation.

chapters.n: They are neither cold nor hot. Laodicea piped in lukewarm water from distant springs, unlike nearby Hierapolis’s hot springs or Colossae’s cold water.

f.g: Spiritually indifferent—useless for either refreshing or healing.

chapters.n: Because they are lukewarm, Christ will spit them out—a vivid picture of how He views spiritual complacency.

f.g: Spew, vomit.

chapters.n: They think they’re rich and need nothing, not realizing they are spiritually miserable, poor, blind, and naked. Laodicea was a wealthy banking city.
Christ’s counsel plays on Laodicea’s famous banks, wool, and eye medicine: buy from Him true gold, white clothes to cover your shame, and salve so you can truly see.

f.g: Laodicea had a medical school known for an eye ointment.

chapters.n: Correction is a sign of His love. Christ disciplines those He loves, so be earnest and repent.

f.w: As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten

chapters.n: A tender invitation: Christ stands knocking at the door. Anyone who hears and opens will enjoy close fellowship with Him, like sharing a meal.

f.w: I stand at the door, and knock

f.g: Eat the evening meal.

chapters.n: Overcomers will sit with Christ on His throne, just as He overcame and sat with His Father on His throne—a promise of exaltation.

f.w: sit with me in my throne

chapters.n: The seventh and final call: listen to what the Spirit says to the churches.
The vision shifts from the churches on earth to heaven. A door opens, and the trumpet-like voice invites John up to see what will happen in the future.

f.w: a door was opened in heaven

chapters.n: Instantly in the Spirit, John sees God’s throne—the center of all authority in the universe—with God seated upon it.
John describes God’s glory in terms of dazzling gems—jasper and carnelian—with an emerald-green rainbow surrounding the throne, recalling God’s covenant with Noah.

f.g: Sardius or carnelian, a reddish gem.

chapters.n: Around the throne sit twenty-four elders in white with golden crowns. Latter-day Saint revelation identifies them as faithful elders from the seven churches who had died and were in God’s paradise.
Lightning and thunder flash from the throne, as at Sinai, and seven lamps of fire burn before it, representing the seven Spirits of God.
Before the throne lies a crystal-clear sea of glass. Latter-day Saint revelation teaches this is the earth in its sanctified, celestial state. Four living creatures full of eyes surround the throne.

f.g: Living creatures, not wild animals.

chapters.n: The four creatures resemble a lion, an ox, a man, and a flying eagle—representing wild beasts, domestic animals, humans, and birds. All creation worships God.

f.g: A young ox or bull.

chapters.n: Each creature has six wings and is full of eyes, and day and night they praise God as holy, eternal, and Almighty. D&C 77 explains the eyes as light and knowledge and the wings as power to act.
Whenever the creatures give glory, honor, and thanks to the eternal God on the throne—
the elders bow down and worship, throwing their crowns before the throne. They acknowledge that all their honor comes from God.

f.g: A gesture of complete submission, like vassal kings honoring an emperor.

chapters.n: They sing that God is worthy of glory, honor, and power because He created everything, and all things exist by His will.

f.g: By your will.

chapters.n: In God’s right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals. Latter-day Saint revelation explains it contains God’s will and works for the earth’s seven thousand years of temporal existence.

f.w: written within and on the backside

chapters.n: A mighty angel calls out: who is worthy to break the seals and open the scroll?
No one anywhere—in heaven, on earth, or in the world of the dead—could open it or even look inside.

f.g: The realm of the dead.

chapters.n: John wept bitterly, because if no one could open the scroll, God’s plan for the world seemed stalled.
An elder comforts him: the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed and can open the scroll. These are royal titles for the Messiah.

f.w: Lion of the tribe of Juda

chapters.n: John turns to see the Lion—and sees a Lamb that looks slaughtered. Christ conquers through His sacrifice. The JST describes twelve horns and twelve eyes, representing the twelve servants of God.

f.w: Lamb as it had been slain

f.g: Horns symbolize power; seven, completeness.

chapters.n: The Lamb steps forward and takes the scroll from the right hand of the One on the throne. Only Christ can carry out the Father’s plan.
The creatures and elders fall before the Lamb with harps and golden bowls of incense, which represent the prayers of the Saints. Our prayers are precious in heaven.

f.g: Golden bowls of incense.

chapters.n: They sing a new song: the Lamb is worthy because He was slain and, by His blood, redeemed people from every family, language, people, and nation.

f.w: redeemed us to God by thy blood

chapters.n: He has made them kings and priests to God, and they will reign on the earth—a hint of the coming Millennium.
John hears countless angels—“ten thousand times ten thousand”—surrounding the throne.
They proclaim loudly that the slain Lamb is worthy of seven honors: power, riches, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and blessing.
Then every creature in all creation joins in, praising both the Father on the throne and the Lamb forever.
The four creatures say “Amen,” and the elders fall down in worship. Heaven’s worship scene is complete.

f.g: Hebrew — ‘so be it,’ ‘truly.’

chapters.n: The Lamb opens the first seal. Latter-day Saint revelation teaches each seal stands for one thousand years of earth’s history, so the first seal covers roughly Adam’s era. A creature thunders, “Come and see.”
A rider on a white horse goes out with a bow and a crown, conquering. Interpretations vary; some Latter-day Saints connect the victorious rider with Enoch’s righteous era.

f.g: White often symbolizes victory and righteousness.

chapters.n: The second seal opens, and the second creature calls, “Come and see.”
A red horse goes out; its rider takes peace from the earth so people kill each other. Red suggests bloodshed—fitting the violent age before the Flood.

f.g: Symbol of war and slaughter.

chapters.n: The third seal opens, revealing a black horse whose rider holds a pair of scales—a symbol of scarcity and rationing.

f.g: Scales for weighing food in time of shortage.

chapters.n: A voice announces famine prices: a day’s wage buys only one quart of wheat or three of barley—yet the oil and wine are not to be harmed.

f.g: Greek denarius — about a day’s wages for a laborer.
About a quart—roughly one person’s daily ration.

chapters.n: The fourth seal opens, and the fourth creature calls, “Come and see.”
A pale, sickly green horse appears, ridden by Death, with Hades following. They are given power over a quarter of the earth through war, famine, disease, and wild beasts.

f.g: Greek chlōros — greenish-gray, the color of a corpse.
Hades, the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: At the fifth seal, John sees under the altar the souls of martyrs who were killed for God’s word. Many connect this era with the meridian of time and the early Christian martyrs.

f.g: In temple sacrifice, blood was poured at the base of the altar.

chapters.n: The martyrs cry out, asking how long until God brings justice for their deaths. It is a cry for righteous judgment, not revenge.
They each receive white robes and are told to rest a little longer, until the full number of fellow servants who will be martyred is complete.

f.w: rest yet for a little season

chapters.n: At the sixth seal there is a great earthquake; the sun turns black like coarse goat-hair cloth, and the moon turns red as blood. These are signs of the last days.

f.g: Rough, dark cloth worn in mourning.

chapters.n: Stars fall to earth like unripe figs shaken from a tree in a storm.

f.g: Late or unripe winter figs that drop easily.

chapters.n: The sky rolls up like a scroll, and every mountain and island is moved. The whole created order seems to come apart.
Everyone—kings, nobles, the wealthy, generals, the powerful, slaves and free—hides in caves and among the rocks. Rank means nothing before God.
They beg the mountains to fall on them and hide them from God and from the Lamb’s wrath.
The great day of their wrath has come—who can stand? Chapter 7 answers: those sealed by God.

f.w: who shall be able to stand

chapters.n: Before more judgments fall, John sees four angels at the four corners of the earth holding back the winds of destruction. D&C 77 says they have power over the earth’s four quarters to save life or destroy.
Another angel rises from the east carrying God’s seal and cries out to the four angels. D&C 77 identifies him as Elias, who comes to gather Israel and restore all things.

f.w: another angel ascending from the east

f.g: A signet ring’s mark showing ownership and protection.

chapters.n: He commands: don’t harm the earth, sea, or trees until God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads, marking them as belonging to Him.

f.w: sealed the servants of our God in their foreheads

chapters.n: John hears that 144,000 from all Israel’s tribes are sealed. D&C 77 explains these are high priests ordained from every nation to bring people to the Church of the Firstborn.

f.w: an hundred and forty and four thousand

chapters.n: Twelve thousand are sealed from each tribe. Judah is listed first, likely because the Messiah came from Judah. Twelve times twelve times a thousand suggests fulness and completeness.

f.g: Judah.

chapters.n: The list continues with Asher, Naphtali, and Manasseh, using Greek spellings of the Hebrew names.

f.g: Asher.
Naphtali.
Manasseh, son of Joseph.

chapters.n: Simeon, Levi, and Issachar follow. Levi, usually left out of land lists because it had no territory, is included here.
Zebulun, Joseph, and Benjamin complete the twelve. Dan is not listed; the reason is unknown, though many guesses have been made.

f.g: Zebulun.
Here probably standing for Ephraim, whose name is otherwise missing.

chapters.n: Then John sees an uncountable multitude from every nation, family, people, and language, standing before the throne in white robes, waving palm branches of victory.

f.g: Symbols of victory and celebration.

chapters.n: They cry out that salvation belongs to God and to the Lamb—it is His gift, not their achievement.
All the angels, elders, and living creatures fall on their faces and worship God.
They praise God with seven words of honor—blessing, glory, wisdom, thanksgiving, honor, power, and might—forever.
An elder asks John who these white-robed people are and where they came from—a teaching question.
John defers to him, and the elder explains: they came through great tribulation and washed their robes white in the Lamb’s blood. Christ’s Atonement makes people clean.

f.w: made them white in the blood of the Lamb

chapters.n: That is why they serve God day and night in His temple, and He will dwell among them, sheltering them with His presence.

f.g: Literally ‘spread His tabernacle over them.’

chapters.n: They will never again suffer hunger, thirst, or scorching heat—words from Isaiah about the redeemed.
The Lamb will be their Shepherd, guiding them to springs of living water, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
When the seventh seal—the earth’s seventh thousand years—is opened, heaven falls silent for about half an hour. The pause builds suspense before the final events. The D&C also foretells this silence.
Seven angels who stand before God are given seven trumpets. Trumpets in Israel announced battles, festivals, and God’s presence.
Another angel stands at the golden altar with a golden censer and much incense, offering it with the prayers of all the Saints.

f.g: A pan for carrying burning coals and incense.

chapters.n: The fragrant smoke rises before God together with the Saints’ prayers. God hears the pleas of His people, including the martyrs’ cry in chapter 6.
The angel fills the censer with fire from the altar and hurls it to the earth, bringing thunder, lightning, and earthquake. The prayers of the Saints set judgment in motion.
The seven angels get ready to blow their trumpets. Latter-day Saint revelation says these trumpets mark God’s work in preparing for Christ’s coming.
The first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, burning a third of the trees and all green grass—echoing the plague of hail in Egypt.

f.g: Judgments here are partial—a warning, not yet the end.

chapters.n: The second trumpet: something like a huge burning mountain is thrown into the sea, and a third of the sea turns to blood, recalling the Nile turned to blood.
A third of sea creatures die and a third of ships are destroyed—striking at trade and food alike.
The third trumpet: a great star blazing like a torch falls on a third of the rivers and springs.

f.g: Torch.

chapters.n: The star is named Wormwood, a bitter plant. It poisons a third of the waters, and many die. In the Old Testament wormwood symbolizes bitterness and judgment.

f.g: A bitter herb (Artemisia).

chapters.n: The fourth trumpet: a third of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, so a third of each day and night has no light—like the plague of darkness in Egypt.

f.g: Struck.

chapters.n: An eagle—or angel—flies overhead crying three woes on the earth’s inhabitants, because the last three trumpets will be even worse.

f.g: Many manuscripts read ‘eagle’ instead of ‘angel.’

chapters.n: At the fifth trumpet, John sees a star that has fallen from heaven to earth—a fallen being—given the key to the bottomless pit. Many see this as Satan or one of his angels.

f.g: Greek abyssos — the abyss, a prison for evil powers.

chapters.n: When the pit opens, smoke pours out like a giant furnace, darkening the sun and sky.
Out of the smoke come locusts with the power to sting like scorpions. Locust swarms were among the most feared disasters of the ancient world.
Unlike normal locusts, they don’t touch plants. They may harm only people who lack God’s seal on their foreheads—God protects His own.

f.w: seal of God in their foreheads

chapters.n: They are allowed to torment, not kill, for five months—roughly the lifespan of a locust. Their sting is like a scorpion’s.

f.g: Possibly the length of a locust season; a limited time.

chapters.n: The suffering will be so intense that people will long to die but won’t be able to.
The locusts look like war horses, wearing what seem to be golden crowns, with faces like humans—a nightmarish army.
They have hair like women’s and teeth like lions’—combining attraction and ferocity.
Their chests look armored with iron, and their wings roar like many chariots charging into battle.
Their scorpion-like tails can hurt people for five months.
Their king is the angel of the abyss, named Abaddon in Hebrew and Apollyon in Greek—both meaning “Destroyer.”

f.g: Hebrew ‘destruction.’
Greek ‘destroyer.’

chapters.n: The first woe is over; two more are coming.
The sixth trumpet sounds, and a voice speaks from the four horns of the golden altar where the Saints’ prayers were offered.

f.w: four horns of the golden altar

chapters.n: The voice orders the release of four angels bound at the Euphrates River, the ancient eastern frontier from which invading armies like Assyria and Babylon came.
These angels had been prepared for an exact hour, day, month, and year—God is in control of timing—to kill a third of mankind.

f.w: an hour, and a day, and a month, and a year
f.g: Shows a precisely appointed time set by God.

chapters.n: The cavalry numbers two hundred million—a number meant to overwhelm the imagination.
The riders wear breastplates colored fiery red, dark blue, and sulfur yellow. The horses have lion-like heads and breathe fire, smoke, and sulfur.

f.g: A dark blue or smoky color.
Sulfur, associated with judgment.

chapters.n: These three plagues—fire, smoke, and sulfur—kill a third of humanity.
Their power is in their mouths and their snake-like tails, which also wound.
Tragically, the survivors still refuse to repent. They keep worshipping demons and lifeless idols that cannot see, hear, or walk.

f.w: neither can see, nor hear, nor walk

chapters.n: Nor do they turn from murder, sorcery, sexual immorality, or theft. The judgments were meant to call people to repentance, but hard hearts resist.

f.g: Greek pharmakeia — magic, often with drugs or potions.

chapters.n: Between the sixth and seventh trumpets comes an interlude. A mighty angel descends, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, a face like the sun, and legs like pillars of fire.
He holds a small open scroll and plants one foot on the sea and one on the land—his message concerns the whole world.

f.g: A small scroll, already unsealed.

chapters.n: He shouts like a roaring lion, and seven thunders speak in reply.
John was about to write what the thunders said, but a heavenly voice told him to seal it up. Not everything God reveals is meant to be published.
The angel raises his hand to heaven, the gesture of a solemn oath.
He swears by the eternal Creator that there will be no more delay. Latter-day Saint scripture also speaks of an angel proclaiming that “there shall be time no longer.”

f.g: No more delay.

chapters.n: When the seventh angel sounds, God’s mysterious plan, announced through His prophets, will be completed.
The heavenly voice tells John to take the open scroll from the angel.
The angel tells him to eat it: it will taste sweet as honey but turn bitter in his stomach. God’s word is sweet to receive, but its message of judgment is hard to bear.
John eats it, and it is exactly as promised—sweet, then bitter. D&C 77 explains the little book represents John’s mission to help gather Israel.
John must prophesy again to many peoples, nations, languages, and kings. Latter-day Saints believe John was allowed to remain on earth to keep ministering until Christ returns.
John is given a measuring rod and told to measure God’s temple, its altar, and the worshippers. Measuring marks something as protected and belonging to God.

f.g: A measuring rod about ten feet long.

chapters.n: He must leave out the outer court, which is given to the nations, who will trample Jerusalem for forty-two months—three and a half years, a symbolic time of trouble.

f.g: 3½ years, half of seven—a limited period of distress.

chapters.n: God will empower two witnesses to prophesy for 1,260 days, wearing sackcloth. Latter-day Saint revelation says these are two prophets raised up to the Jewish nation in the last days.

f.w: a thousand two hundred and threescore days
f.g: 1,260 days—about 3½ years.

chapters.n: They are the two olive trees and two lampstands of Zechariah’s vision—anointed servants who shine God’s light.
Anyone who tries to harm them will be consumed by fire from their mouths, as with Elijah. God protects His witnesses until their work is done.

f.w: fire proceedeth out of their mouth

chapters.n: Like Elijah, they can stop the rain; like Moses, they can turn water to blood and bring plagues.
When their testimony is finished, the beast from the abyss will fight them, overcome them, and kill them.

f.w: beast that ascendeth out of the bottomless pit

chapters.n: Their bodies will lie in the street of the great city, spiritually called Sodom and Egypt for its wickedness, where the Lord was crucified—Jerusalem.

f.w: where also our Lord was crucified
f.g: Identifies the city as Jerusalem.

chapters.n: For three and a half days people from many nations will stare at their bodies and refuse to let them be buried—a terrible insult in the ancient world.
The world will celebrate and exchange gifts because these prophets had troubled them with calls to repent.
After three and a half days, God’s breath of life enters them and they stand up, terrifying those who see. Their resurrection echoes Christ’s.
A loud voice calls them up, and they ascend to heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch.

f.w: ascended up to heaven in a cloud

chapters.n: At that moment a great earthquake topples a tenth of the city and kills seven thousand. The survivors are terrified and give glory to God.
The second woe is past; the third is coming soon.
The seventh trumpet sounds, and heaven announces the climax: the world’s kingdom has become the kingdom of our Lord and His Christ, and He will reign forever.
The twenty-four elders fall on their faces and worship God.
They thank God Almighty for taking His great power and beginning His reign.
The nations raged, but now God’s judgment has come: the dead will be judged, His servants the prophets and Saints rewarded, and those who destroy the earth destroyed.
God’s temple in heaven opens, revealing the ark of His covenant, with lightning, thunder, earthquake, and hail. God’s presence and covenant faithfulness are on full display.

f.g: The ark of the covenant.

chapters.n: A great sign appears in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet, and a crown of twelve stars. Joseph Smith’s inspired translation identifies her as the Church of God; the twelve stars recall Israel’s tribes.

f.w: a woman clothed with the sun
f.g: JST Revelation 12 explains the woman as the church of God.

chapters.n: She is pregnant and cries out in the pain of labor—a picture of God’s people longing for God’s kingdom to be born.
A second sign: a huge red dragon with seven heads, ten horns, and seven crowns—a monstrous image of Satan’s power over earthly kingdoms.

The dragon’s tail sweeps away a third of heaven’s stars. Latter-day Saints see here the third of God’s spirit children who followed Satan in the premortal rebellion. He waits to devour the woman’s child.

She bears a son destined to rule the nations with an iron scepter, and he is caught up to God’s throne. The JST identifies the child as the kingdom of God and His Christ; many also see Christ Himself.

f.g: JST Revelation 12:7 calls the child ‘the kingdom of our God and his Christ.’

chapters.n: The woman flees into the wilderness to a place God prepared, where she is cared for 1,260 days. Latter-day Saints see the Church withdrawing during the Great Apostasy until its restoration.
War breaks out in heaven: Michael and his angels battle the dragon and his angels. Latter-day Saints understand this as the premortal conflict over God’s plan and agency.

f.g: The archangel, identified in Latter-day Saint teaching as Adam.

chapters.n: The dragon loses and has no place in heaven any longer.
The great dragon—the ancient serpent called the Devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world—is thrown down to earth with his angels.

f.g: Devil = ‘slanderer’ (Greek); Satan = ‘adversary’ (Hebrew).

chapters.n: A voice in heaven celebrates: salvation and God’s kingdom have come, for the accuser who charged the believers day and night has been thrown down.
The faithful defeat Satan by the Lamb’s blood and by their testimony, and they don’t cling to life even when facing death. Christ’s Atonement and our witness overcome evil.
Heaven rejoices, but woe to the earth: the devil has come down full of rage because he knows his time is short.
Thrown down to earth, the dragon pursues the woman who bore the child—Satan attacks the Church.
She is given eagle’s wings to fly to her wilderness refuge, where she is sustained for “a time, and times, and half a time”—three and a half years.

f.w: a time, and times, and half a time

chapters.n: The serpent spews a flood of water after her to sweep her away—perhaps floods of lies and persecution.
But the earth opens and swallows the flood, helping the woman. God uses even creation to protect His people.
Furious, the dragon goes to war against the rest of her children—those who keep God’s commandments and hold the testimony of Jesus. This describes the faithful in the latter days.
Standing by the sea, John sees a beast rise from it with seven heads and ten crowned horns, with blasphemous names on its heads. It represents oppressive earthly power that defies God.

f.w: beast rise up out of the sea

f.g: Titles claiming divine honors, like those Roman emperors took.

chapters.n: It combines a leopard, bear, and lion—the beasts of Daniel’s vision of world empires. The dragon gives it his power, throne, and authority.

f.w: the dragon gave him his power

chapters.n: One head seems mortally wounded, yet the wound heals, and the whole world follows the beast in amazement. Evil mimics Christ’s death and resurrection.

f.g: A counterfeit of the Lamb ‘as it had been slain.’

chapters.n: People worship the dragon and the beast, asking, “Who can fight it?” This parodies Israel’s praise, “Who is like unto thee, O Lord?”

f.w: Who is like unto the beast

chapters.n: The beast is given a boastful, blasphemous mouth and authority for forty-two months—a limited time allowed by God.
It slanders God, His name, His dwelling, and those who live in heaven.

f.g: God’s dwelling place.

chapters.n: It is permitted to make war on the Saints and overcome them, gaining authority over every people and nation. Nephi saw a similar latter-day force fighting the Lamb’s Church.
Everyone whose name is not in the Lamb’s book of life will worship it. Christ is the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world—His sacrifice was planned before creation.

f.w: Lamb slain from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Anyone who has ears should listen carefully.
Those destined for captivity will go into captivity; those who kill by the sword will die by it. Saints should endure faithfully rather than fight back with violence.

f.g: Steadfast endurance.

chapters.n: A second beast rises from the land. It looks like a lamb with two horns but speaks like a dragon—a false religious power that appears gentle but serves Satan.

f.g: Called the ‘false prophet’ later.

chapters.n: It uses the first beast’s full authority and makes the world worship that beast.
It performs great signs, even calling down fire from heaven in public—imitating Elijah to win belief.
By these miracles it deceives earth’s inhabitants and tells them to make an image honoring the beast that was wounded by the sword yet lived.
It gives breath to the image so it can speak and orders death for those who refuse to worship it—like Nebuchadnezzar’s golden statue.
It forces everyone—small and great, rich and poor, free and slave—to receive a mark on the right hand or forehead, counterfeiting God’s seal on His servants.

f.g: Greek charagma — a stamp or brand showing ownership.

chapters.n: No one can buy or sell without the mark, the beast’s name, or its number—economic pressure to conform.
The beast’s number is 666, “the number of a man.” Many scholars think it encodes a name, possibly Nero, using letter-values; others note six falls short of seven, the number of perfection.

f.g: 666; in Hebrew and Greek, letters doubled as numbers.

chapters.n: In contrast to the beasts, John sees the Lamb standing on Mount Zion with the 144,000, who bear His and His Father’s name on their foreheads rather than the beast’s mark.

f.w: Father's name written in their foreheads

chapters.n: A sound from heaven roars like rushing water and thunder, mixed with the music of harpists.
They sing a new song before the throne that only the 144,000 redeemed could learn. Some truths can be learned only through experience and covenant.
They are pure and undefiled, follow the Lamb wherever He goes, and are the firstfruits offered to God and the Lamb. “Virgins” here describes spiritual faithfulness, not a ban on marriage.

f.g: A symbol of moral and spiritual purity—undefiled by idolatry.

chapters.n: No deceit is found in their mouths; they stand blameless before God.

John sees an angel flying through heaven with the everlasting gospel for every nation, family, language, and people. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in the Restoration, including Moroni’s visits and the coming forth of the Book of Mormon.
The angel calls out: fear God, glorify Him, and worship the Creator, because the hour of His judgment has come.

f.w: Fear God, and give glory to him

chapters.n: A second angel announces that Babylon has fallen—the great city that made all nations drink the intoxicating wine of her immorality. Babylon stands for the world’s wickedness.
A third angel warns: anyone who worships the beast and its image and accepts its mark—
—will drink the undiluted wine of God’s anger and suffer fire and sulfur before the holy angels and the Lamb.

f.g: Full strength—ancient wine was usually diluted with water.

chapters.n: The smoke of their torment rises forever, and they have no rest day or night. Scripture uses such images to show the seriousness of choosing evil.
Here is why the Saints must endure: they keep God’s commandments and remain faithful to Jesus.
A voice tells John to write: blessed are those who die in the Lord from now on. They rest from their labors, and their good works go with them.
Now come harvest images. One like the Son of Man, crowned with gold, sits on a white cloud holding a sharp sickle.

f.g: A curved blade for cutting grain.

chapters.n: An angel from the temple calls out: put in your sickle and reap, for the earth’s harvest is fully ripe.

f.w: harvest of the earth is ripe

chapters.n: The One on the cloud swings His sickle, and the earth is harvested—often seen as gathering the righteous.
Another angel comes from the heavenly temple, also carrying a sharp sickle.
An angel with authority over fire comes from the altar and calls: gather the grape clusters of the earth’s vine, for they are ripe.
The angel gathers the grapes and throws them into the great winepress of God’s wrath—an image of judgment on the wicked.

f.w: winepress of the wrath of God

chapters.n: The winepress is trampled outside the city, and blood flows as high as a horse’s bridle for about 180 miles—a vivid, exaggerated picture of total judgment.

f.w: a thousand and six hundred furlongs
f.g: A furlong (stadion) was about 600 feet; 1,600 is roughly 180-200 miles.

chapters.n: John sees another great sign: seven angels holding the seven last plagues, which complete God’s judgment on unrepentant wickedness.

f.g: Completed, brought to an end.

chapters.n: He sees a sea of glass mixed with fire, and on it stand those who conquered the beast, its image, and its mark, holding harps from God.
Like Israel singing beside the Red Sea after escaping Egypt, they sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb: God’s works are great and His ways just and true.

f.g: Many manuscripts read ‘King of the nations.’

chapters.n: Who will not revere and glorify God? Only He is holy, and all nations will come and worship Him because His righteous judgments have been revealed.
Then John sees the heavenly temple—the tabernacle of the testimony—opened.

f.g: The tent housing the ark and the tablets of the covenant.

chapters.n: The seven angels come out wearing pure white linen and golden sashes, dressed like priests. Their judgments are a holy act.
One of the four living creatures hands them seven golden bowls filled with the wrath of the eternal God.

f.g: Wide, shallow bowls used in temple service.

chapters.n: The temple fills with smoke from God’s glory and power, and no one can enter until the seven plagues are finished—as when God’s glory filled Solomon’s temple.

f.w: filled with smoke from the glory of God

chapters.n: A loud voice from the temple sends the seven angels to pour out their bowls of God’s wrath on the earth. These plagues echo those on Egypt but now affect the whole world.
The first bowl brings painful, festering sores on those who bear the beast’s mark and worship its image—like the boils of Egypt.

f.g: Foul, painful ulcers.

chapters.n: The second bowl turns the sea to blood like a corpse’s, and every living thing in it dies.

f.g: Thick, clotted blood.

chapters.n: The third bowl turns rivers and springs to blood.
The angel over the waters declares that God is righteous in these judgments.
Those who shed the blood of Saints and prophets are given blood to drink—a punishment that fits the crime.
A voice from the altar—where the martyrs had cried for justice—agrees: God’s judgments are true and right.

f.w: true and righteous are thy judgments

chapters.n: The fourth bowl is poured on the sun, giving it power to scorch people with fire.
People are burned by intense heat yet curse God, who controls these plagues, and refuse to repent and honor Him.
The fifth bowl is poured on the beast’s throne, and his kingdom falls into darkness. People gnaw their tongues in agony.

f.g: The beast’s throne or seat of power.

chapters.n: Still they curse the God of heaven for their pain and sores and do not turn from their deeds.
The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates, clearing a path for the kings from the east. The drying recalls the Red Sea and Jordan crossings, now used for an invasion.
Three foul spirits like frogs come from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet—a counterfeit trinity spreading deception.

f.g: The second beast of chapter 13.

chapters.n: These demonic spirits perform signs and go to the rulers of the world, gathering them for battle on the great day of God Almighty.
Jesus interrupts with a warning: He will come like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes on, so he won’t be caught naked and ashamed.
The armies gather at a place called in Hebrew Armageddon—likely “mountain of Megiddo,” a valley in northern Israel famous for ancient battles.

f.g: Hebrew Har Megiddo, ‘mountain of Megiddo.’

chapters.n: The seventh bowl is poured into the air, and a loud voice from God’s throne declares, “It is done.”
Lightning, thunder, and the greatest earthquake in human history follow.
The great city splits into three parts, the cities of the nations collapse, and God remembers Babylon to give her the cup of His fierce wrath.
Islands vanish and mountains disappear—the landscape itself is transformed.
Enormous hailstones weighing about a talent each—roughly 75 to 100 pounds—fall on people, who curse God for the terrible plague.

f.g: A unit of weight, very roughly 75-100 pounds.

chapters.n: One of the seven bowl angels invites John to see the judgment of the “great whore” who sits on many waters. She symbolizes a seductive, corrupt world system opposed to God.

f.g: A prophetic image of spiritual unfaithfulness and corruption.

chapters.n: Earth’s rulers have committed spiritual adultery with her, and its people are drunk on the wine of her immorality.
In the Spirit, John is carried into the wilderness and sees a woman sitting on a scarlet beast covered with blasphemous names, with seven heads and ten horns.
She wears purple and scarlet, the colors of royalty and luxury, and glitters with gold, jewels, and pearls. Her golden cup is full of abominations and filth.
Her forehead bears a name: “Mystery, Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots and Abominations of the Earth.” Some Roman prostitutes wore their names on headbands.
She is drunk on the blood of the Saints and of Jesus’s martyrs. John is astonished at what he sees.

f.w: drunken with the blood of the saints

f.g: Amazement, astonishment—not approval.

chapters.n: The angel asks why John is amazed and promises to explain the mystery of the woman and the beast carrying her.
The beast “was, and is not,” and will rise from the abyss before going to destruction. This mocks God, “which is, and which was, and which is to come.” The world will marvel at it.

f.g: Destruction, ruin.

chapters.n: Wisdom is needed: the seven heads are seven mountains where the woman sits. Ancient readers would think of Rome, the city on seven hills.

f.g: Rome was famously built on seven hills.

chapters.n: They are also seven kings: five have fallen, one now reigns, and one has not yet come and will rule only briefly.
The beast itself is an eighth king, belonging to the seven, and it heads to destruction.
The ten horns are ten kings who don’t yet have kingdoms but will rule with the beast for a short “hour.”
These kings are united in purpose and hand their power to the beast.
They will war against the Lamb, but the Lamb—Lord of lords and King of kings—will conquer them, along with His called, chosen, and faithful followers.

f.w: Lord of lords, and King of kings

chapters.n: The waters where she sits are peoples, crowds, nations, and languages—her influence is worldwide.
In a twist, the beast and the ten kings will turn on the woman, strip her, devour her, and burn her. Evil ultimately destroys itself.
God put this into their hearts to accomplish His purpose until His words are fulfilled. Even the wicked cannot thwart God’s plan.
The woman is the great city that rules over earth’s kings—in John’s day, Rome; in every age, the proud power of worldliness.
Another powerful angel descends, and his glory lights up the earth.

He shouts that Babylon the Great has fallen. Once glamorous, she is now a ruin haunted by demons, foul spirits, and unclean birds—language from Isaiah’s and Jeremiah’s oracles against ancient Babylon.
All nations drank her intoxicating wine; kings committed immorality with her; merchants grew rich from her excessive luxury.

f.g: Luxury, extravagant living.

chapters.n: A voice from heaven calls: “Come out of her, my people,” so you don’t share in her sins or her plagues. Latter-day revelation repeats this call to leave spiritual Babylon.

f.w: Come out of her, my people

chapters.n: Her sins are piled up to heaven, and God has remembered her crimes.
Pay her back as she has done—double for her deeds. “Double” is a Hebrew idiom for full repayment.
Give her torment equal to her self-glorifying luxury. She boasts, “I sit as a queen; I am no widow and will never know sorrow.”

f.g: Lived in arrogant luxury.

chapters.n: So her plagues—death, mourning, and famine—will come in a single day, and she will be burned, because the Lord God who judges her is mighty.
The kings who shared her luxury will weep when they see the smoke of her burning.
They stand far off in fear, crying, “Alas, alas, great city Babylon! In one hour your judgment has come.”

f.g: Emphasizes how sudden her collapse is.

chapters.n: The merchants mourn too—not for her, but because no one buys their goods anymore.

f.w: merchants of the earth shall weep

chapters.n: John lists her luxury trade: gold, silver, jewels, pearls, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, fragrant citron wood, ivory, costly wood, bronze, iron, and marble.

f.g: Fragrant citron wood from North Africa, prized for expensive tables.
Dye from murex shells—extremely costly.

chapters.n: The list ends shockingly: spices, perfumes, food, livestock, chariots, slaves—and human souls. A system that sells people has lost its soul.

f.g: Literally ‘bodies’—human beings treated as cargo.

chapters.n: The luxuries she craved are gone; all her elegance and splendor have vanished forever.

f.g: Rich, luxurious.

chapters.n: The merchants who grew rich from her stand at a distance, weeping and wailing in fear.
They cry, “Alas, the great city, dressed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet, glittering with gold, jewels, and pearls!”
In one hour all that wealth is gone. Sea captains, sailors, and traders watch from afar.

f.g: Ship’s captain or pilot.

chapters.n: Seeing the smoke, they cry, “What city was ever like this great city?”

f.w: What city is like unto this great city

chapters.n: Throwing dust on their heads in grief, they lament that the city that made them rich is destroyed in one hour.

f.g: An ancient sign of mourning.

chapters.n: But heaven, the Saints, Apostles, and prophets are called to rejoice, for God has brought justice for them.
A mighty angel hurls a huge millstone into the sea: Babylon will be thrown down violently and never be found again.
No more music, no craftsmen, no sound of the millstone grinding grain—ordinary life in her streets falls silent.
No lamp will shine and no wedding joy will be heard. Her merchants were the world’s powerful, and her sorceries deceived every nation.

f.w: voice of the bridegroom and of the bride

f.g: Magic and deceptive enchantments.

chapters.n: In her was found the blood of prophets, Saints, and all who were killed on earth. Her judgment is just.

After Babylon’s fall, a vast crowd in heaven shouts “Alleluia”—“Praise the Lord”—giving salvation, glory, honor, and power to God. This chapter contains the only uses of “Alleluia” in the New Testament.

f.g: Greek form of Hebrew Hallelujah, ‘Praise ye the LORD.’

chapters.n: God’s judgments are true and right: He judged the great harlot who corrupted the earth and avenged His servants’ blood.

f.w: avenged the blood of his servants

chapters.n: Again they shout “Alleluia,” for the smoke of her ruin rises forever—her fall is final.
The twenty-four elders and four living creatures bow and worship, saying, “Amen. Alleluia!”
A voice from the throne calls all God’s servants, great and small, to praise Him.
A sound like a vast crowd, crashing waters, and booming thunder cries: “Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.” Handel set these words in his famous Hallelujah Chorus.

f.g: All-powerful.

chapters.n: Rejoice and give Him glory, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has prepared herself. Scripture often pictures Christ as the Bridegroom and His people as the bride.
The bride is given fine linen, bright and clean, which stands for the righteous acts of the Saints—made possible by grace.

f.g: Righteous deeds of the Saints.

chapters.n: The angel tells John to write: blessed are those invited to the Lamb’s wedding feast. These are God’s true words.
John falls to worship the angel, who stops him: “I am a fellow servant—worship God.” The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy: every true prophet bears witness of Christ.

f.w: the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy

chapters.n: Heaven opens, and Christ rides out on a white horse. He is called Faithful and True, and He judges and makes war in righteousness—this is His Second Coming.

f.g: A symbol of victory.

chapters.n: His eyes blaze like fire, He wears many crowns, and He has a name known only to Himself.

f.g: Greek diadēmata — royal crowns, showing supreme kingship.

chapters.n: His robe is dipped in blood, and His name is the Word of God. Latter-day revelation says He will come in red apparel, recalling both His Atonement and His judgment.
The armies of heaven follow Him on white horses, dressed in clean white linen—they come with Him, not to fight in their own strength.
A sharp sword—His word—comes from His mouth to strike the nations. He will rule with an iron scepter and tread the winepress of God’s fierce wrath.
On His robe and thigh is written His title: King of kings and Lord of lords.

f.w: KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS

chapters.n: An angel standing in the sun summons the birds to “the supper of the great God”—a grim contrast to the Lamb’s wedding supper.
The birds will feast on the bodies of kings, commanders, warriors, horses, and all people who fought against God. Rank offers no protection.
The beast, earth’s kings, and their armies gather to fight Christ and His army.
The beast is captured along with the false prophet who deceived people with signs. Both are thrown alive into the lake of fire burning with sulfur.
The rest are slain by the sword from Christ’s mouth—His word alone wins the battle—and the birds are filled.

f.w: sword proceeded out of his mouth

chapters.n: An angel comes down from heaven holding the key to the abyss and a great chain.
He seizes the dragon—the ancient serpent, the Devil, Satan—and binds him for a thousand years. This is the Millennium.

Satan is locked and sealed in the abyss so he can no longer deceive the nations until the thousand years end; then he must be released briefly. The Book of Mormon adds that Satan is bound because of the people’s righteousness.
John sees thrones and those given authority to judge, along with martyrs and all who refused the beast’s mark. They live and reign with Christ a thousand years.

f.w: reigned with Christ a thousand years

chapters.n: The rest of the dead don’t come back to life until the thousand years are over. The faithful rising at Christ’s coming is called the first resurrection.
Those in the first resurrection are blessed and holy. The second death has no power over them; they will be priests of God and Christ and reign with Him a thousand years.
When the thousand years end, Satan will be released from his prison.
He will deceive the nations across the earth—called Gog and Magog—and gather them for battle in numbers like the sand of the sea.

f.g: Names from Ezekiel for hostile northern nations, used here for all God’s enemies.

chapters.n: They spread across the earth and surround the camp of the Saints and the beloved city, but fire from heaven consumes them. D&C calls this the battle of the great God, led by Michael.
The devil is thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur with the beast and false prophet. Satan’s defeat is final and forever.

f.w: the devil that deceived them was cast

chapters.n: John sees a great white throne and the One seated on it. Earth and sky flee from His presence and disappear. The final judgment begins.

f.w: the earth and the heaven fled away

chapters.n: The dead, both great and small, stand before God. Books are opened, including the book of life, and everyone is judged by what is written according to their works. Joseph Smith taught that records kept on earth are part of these books.
The sea gives up its dead, and death and Hades give up theirs. Everyone is resurrected and judged by their deeds—no one is forgotten.

f.w: the sea gave up the dead

f.g: Hades—the spirit realm of the dead.

chapters.n: Death and Hades are themselves thrown into the lake of fire—Christ’s victory ends death forever. This is the second death.

f.w: death and hell were cast into the lake of fire

chapters.n: Anyone not found in the book of life is cast into the lake of fire.

John sees a new heaven and a new earth replacing the old ones, and there is no more sea—the ancient symbol of chaos and danger. Latter-day Saints believe the earth itself will be renewed and become celestial.

f.w: a new heaven and a new earth
f.r: Isaiah 65:17; D&C 29:23-24; D&C 88:17-20; Articles of Faith 1:10

f.g: The sea often symbolized chaos and the source of the beast (13:1).

chapters.n: He sees the holy city, New Jerusalem, descending from God like a bride beautifully dressed for her husband.
A loud voice announces that God’s dwelling is now with people. He will live among them as their God, and they will be His people—the goal of every covenant.

f.w: tabernacle of God is with men

chapters.n: God will wipe every tear from their eyes. Death, grief, crying, and pain will be gone forever, because the old order has passed away.
The One on the throne declares, “Behold, I make all things new,” and tells John to write it down because these words are trustworthy and true.
“It is done.” The Alpha and Omega promises to give freely from the spring of the water of life to anyone who is thirsty.
Whoever overcomes will inherit all things; God will be his God, and he will be His son. Latter-day Saints see here the promise of exaltation as heirs of God.
But cowards, unbelievers, the corrupt, murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and liars who refuse to repent will face the lake of fire—the second death.

f.g: Those who abandon faith out of cowardice.

chapters.n: One of the seven bowl angels invites John to see the bride, the Lamb’s wife—a deliberate contrast to the harlot of chapter 17.
In the Spirit he takes John to a great high mountain and shows him holy Jerusalem descending from God.
The city shines with God’s glory, radiant like a precious jewel, clear as crystal.
It has a high wall with twelve gates guarded by twelve angels, and on the gates are the names of Israel’s twelve tribes.
Three gates face each direction—east, north, south, and west—open to people from every part of the earth.
The wall has twelve foundation stones bearing the names of the Lamb’s twelve Apostles. The Church is built on Israel’s covenant and the Apostles’ witness.
The angel has a golden measuring rod to measure the city, its gates, and its wall.
The city is a perfect cube, about 12,000 furlongs—roughly 1,400 miles—on each side. The Holy of Holies in Solomon’s temple was also a cube; the whole city is God’s holy dwelling.

f.g: Roughly 1,400-1,500 miles.

f.w: length and the breadth and the height of it are equal

chapters.n: The wall measures 144 cubits—about 216 feet—by human measurement, which the angel also used. Again, twelve times twelve signals perfection.

f.w: an hundred and forty and four cubits
f.g: A cubit was about 18 inches.

chapters.n: The wall is made of jasper, and the city is pure gold, so pure it looks like clear glass.

f.w: pure gold, like unto clear glass

chapters.n: The foundations are decorated with every kind of precious stone: jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, and emerald for the first four.

f.g: A milky or agate-like quartz.

chapters.n: The list continues with eight more gems. Many resemble the twelve stones on the high priest’s breastplate, which bore Israel’s tribal names.

f.g: A banded red-and-white onyx.
An apple-green stone.
Possibly a blue or orange-red gem.

chapters.n: Each of the twelve gates is a single pearl—the source of the phrase “pearly gates”—and the main street is gold, transparent as glass.

f.g: several = each individual.

chapters.n: There is no temple in the city, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. God’s presence fills everything.

f.g: The whole city has become a Holy of Holies.

chapters.n: The city needs no sun or moon, because God’s glory lights it and the Lamb is its lamp.
The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it.

f.w: nations of them which are saved

chapters.n: Its gates will never be shut, because there is no night there—no danger and no darkness.

f.w: gates of it shall not be shut

chapters.n: The glory and honor of the nations will be brought into it—the best of every culture, purified.
Nothing impure, nothing shameful or deceitful will enter—only those whose names are written in the Lamb’s book of life.
The angel shows John the river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and the Lamb. Life itself flows from them.

f.w: pure river of water of life

chapters.n: On both sides of the river grows the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, a crop every month, and its leaves heal the nations. What was lost in Eden is restored.
There will be no more curse, as there was after the Fall. God’s and the Lamb’s throne will be there, and His servants will worship and serve Him.
They will see His face—the deepest hope of the faithful—and His name will be on their foreheads.

f.w: his name shall be in their foreheads

chapters.n: No night, no need for lamps or sun, for the Lord God gives them light. They will reign forever.

f.w: the Lord God giveth them light

chapters.n: The angel confirms these words are trustworthy. The God who inspired the prophets sent His angel to show His servants what must soon happen.
Jesus says, “I am coming soon!” Blessed is the one who keeps the words of this prophecy.
John testifies that he personally saw and heard these things. Overwhelmed, he again falls to worship at the angel’s feet.
The angel again stops him: “Don’t do that! I am a fellow servant with you, the prophets, and all who keep this book. Worship God.”
Unlike Daniel, who was told to seal his book, John must not seal this prophecy, because the time is near.
A sober warning: the time is coming when choices become fixed. Those who do wrong will keep doing wrong, and the holy will remain holy. Now is the time to choose.
“I am coming soon,” Jesus repeats, “and My reward is with Me, to repay each person according to his work.”
Jesus declares He is the Alpha and Omega, the beginning and end, the first and last—Lord of all history.
Blessed are those who keep His commandments—many manuscripts read “wash their robes”—so they may have the right to the tree of life and enter the city through its gates.

f.g: Many early manuscripts read ‘wash their robes.’

f.w: right to the tree of life

chapters.n: Outside the city are the “dogs”—a term for the impure—along with sorcerers, the sexually immoral, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and lives a lie.

f.g: A harsh ancient insult for the morally unclean.

chapters.n: Jesus Himself speaks: He sent His angel with this testimony for the churches. He is both the root and descendant of David—David’s Creator and David’s heir—and the bright morning star.

f.w: root and the offspring of David

chapters.n: The Spirit and the bride—the Church—say “Come!” Everyone who hears should say “Come!” Whoever is thirsty may come and take the water of life freely. The Bible nearly closes with an open invitation.

John warns that anyone who adds to this book’s prophecy will receive its plagues. Like Moses’s similar warning, this forbids people from altering God’s word; it does not forbid God from giving further revelation.

f.w: If any man shall add unto these things

chapters.n: And anyone who removes words from this prophecy will lose his share in the tree of life and the holy city. Nephi foresaw that plain and precious parts would be taken from the Bible.
Jesus promises, “Surely I come quickly.” John responds with the prayer of every believer: “Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus.”

f.g: Echoes the early Aramaic prayer Maranatha, ‘Our Lord, come!’

chapters.n: The book ends with grace: may the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

f.w: grace of our Lord Jesus Christ
